The newly announced 18 October show follows overwhelming demand for the group’s initial 17 October concert, which sold out within two hours of general sales opening. Queue numbers for the first day of presales reportedly surpassed 500,000.

items.body:
YE (fka Kanye West) is set make his Indonesian concert debut on 24 October at Gelora Bung Karno (GBK) Main Stadium, bringing his 360-degree Globe Stage to a venue that can hold up to 77,000 fans. The show is currently his only announced Southeast Asian stop, giving Jakarta a rare moment at the centre of his regional touring plans.

For promoter Raw Vision Collective, the concert is bigger than a one-night spectacle. Anchored by CEO Micha Nanda and Chief Marketing Officer Karen Tjahja, the collective sees the show as a chance to prove Jakarta can host major global productions while also drawing attention to the city’s wider creative culture. Early demand suggests that ambition is already travelling, with ticket purchases coming in from across Asia Pacific and beyond, while Category 4 — the most affordable tier — is nearing sell-out.

Here, Raw Vision Collective traces the journey from meeting YE in the U.S. and seeing the Globe Stage firsthand in Kazakhstan to the realities of producing a stadium show with local and international teams. Along the way, the collective reflects on Jakarta’s growing place on the touring map, the value of concert tourism, and what projects like this could mean for Indonesia’s live music ecosystem.

YE LIVE IN JAKARTA is YE's only announced Southeast Asian stop. Can you walk us through how this opportunity first came about?

The opportunity developed over time through conversations, relationships, and trust. We went to the U.S. to meet YE and his team, share our vision for Indonesia, and discuss what it would take to bring a production of this scale to Jakarta. As part of that journey, we also attended YE shows overseas to experience the production firsthand. Most recently, the Raw Vision Collective team travelled to Almaty, Kazakhstan, to see the latest execution of the Globe Stage up close and meet members of YE’s creative circle, including Tony Williams and Andre Troutman. Being there gave us a much clearer understanding of how YE’s live experience comes together, from the Globe Stage and technical elements to the overall production and audience experience, and helped us look more practically at what needs to be prepared locally.

At the same time, we see this relationship as a two-way cultural exchange. While we are learning from YE and his team about the creative vision behind the show, we also want to present YE with a window into Indonesian culture and art. YE has consistently drawn inspiration from different cultures and creative disciplines around the world, from the visual references surrounding BULLY, which draw inspiration from traditional Mexican wrestling, to his appreciation for Japanese art, architecture, and photography, including figures such as Daido Moriyama and Tadao Ando.

Interestingly, there is already a connection to Indonesia. 'Jukebox Joints', YE’s collaboration with A$AP Rocky, samples 'Doa Untuk Kekasih' by Indonesian band Rasela. For us, that creates an interesting starting point to introduce him to even more of Indonesia’s creative heritage. We are preparing a curated selection of Indonesian music, art, and cultural references from different eras to share with YE, and we hope it gives him an opportunity to discover more of the richness of Indonesian culture and perhaps find inspiration that could become part of his future creative work. It is not only about bringing YE’s creative world to Indonesia, but also about showing what Indonesia can bring to the global stage.

At what point did you know this was a realistic possibility rather than just an ambition?

There wasn’t really one single moment where everything suddenly became real. It happened step by step, starting with conversations and relationship-building with YE’s management team. One moment that really stood out was when we were invited to meet YE personally in the U.S. while he was working on a music video. Up until that point, most of our conversations had been with his management, so finally meeting YE directly felt like an important moment in the journey.

During that meeting, YE asked us a very simple but important question: “Why should I come to Jakarta?” That opened up a much more direct conversation about Indonesia, its audience, cultural energy, creative talent, and why we believed Jakarta was capable of delivering a production of this scale. From there, things became increasingly concrete, moving into detailed discussions around production, venue, logistics, technical requirements, and timelines. Seeing the Globe Stage firsthand in Almaty also gave us a much clearer understanding of what would be required to bring that experience to Jakarta. It was really the combination of the personal conversation with YE, the increasingly detailed production discussions, and seeing the show up close that made the opportunity feel much more tangible.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Raw Vision Collective (@rawvision.collective)

So why was Jakarta the right city for this show, and what made Raw Vision Collective the right team to bring it together?

For us, what makes Jakarta exciting is the combination of audience, cultural energy, and scale. Indonesia has a large and highly engaged music audience, supported by a strong creative ecosystem across music, fashion, art, and culture. Jakarta also has the infrastructure needed for a production of this magnitude, with GBK stadium providing the capacity and scale required for a major international stadium show.

Importantly, we see this as an opportunity to showcase what Jakarta and Indonesia can offer as a destination for international live music. We are already seeing interest from overseas markets, including Singapore, Australia, the Philippines, Vietnam, and other countries, which shows that the opportunity extends beyond the domestic audience. Fans travelling for the concert can also experience Jakarta’s food, culture, fashion, hospitality, and creative scene, making the city part of the overall journey.

This reflects what Raw Vision Collective stands for. We believe live music can offer more than a conventional concert experience. As a creative collective, we aim to build cultural experiences that bring together music, art, food, travel, and community in a more immersive and meaningful way. YE was a natural fit for that vision because his work has always gone beyond music, bringing together visual art, fashion, stage design, and storytelling. So for us, YE LIVE IN JAKARTA is not only about bringing a major international artist to Indonesia, but also about showing what Jakarta and Indonesia can offer to audiences and international touring teams.

Were there any moments during the planning process when you thought the concert might not happen?

The very first and most crucial moment was convincing YE that Jakarta was the right place for this show. Once we had that commitment, the focus shifted to bringing that vision to life. Since then, we have been working closely with YE’s team and our Indonesian production professionals to understand the technical requirements and everything it takes to execute a show of this scale. There are a lot of moving parts behind the scenes, from production and logistics to safety and crowd management, and our focus has been on making sure everything comes together seamlessly. At the end of the day, all of that preparation comes down to one thing: giving fans in Jakarta a truly once-in-a-lifetime experience.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by 𝑮𝑼𝑴 (@ihategum)

The Globe Stage has become synonymous with YE’s recent performances. What are some of the biggest logistical and technical challenges of bringing a production like this to Indonesia?

The Globe Stage is definitely one of the elements we are most excited to bring to Jakarta. It has become such a defining part of YE’s recent performances, and experiencing it in person is very different from watching a conventional stadium show. What makes it special is the 360-degree concept. Instead of a traditional front-facing stage, the Globe Stage creates an immersive environment where the production surrounds the audience, bringing together the performance, visuals, lighting, audio, and pyrotechnics as one integrated experience.

Having attended several YE shows overseas, including the recent show in Almaty, we have been able to see firsthand how complex the production is and how every element needs to work together. What audiences see on stage is only one part of the story. From the structure and electrical systems to audio, lighting, special effects, logistics, crowd movement, and safety, every detail has to come together.

A big part of making that happen is the expertise of our Indonesian production teams. They are working closely with YE’s international production team and GBK to bring the production to life here in Jakarta. They understand the local environment, the technical requirements, and what it takes to execute a show of this scale safely and professionally. But our ambition goes beyond delivering the Globe Stage itself. We want YE LIVE IN JAKARTA to feel like a complete experience, especially for fans travelling from outside Indonesia — one that extends beyond the stadium and beyond one night.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Raw Vision Collective (@rawvision.collective)

How much of the production is travelling internationally, and how much is being built or supported by local Indonesian crews?

It is very much a collaborative production, and that is one of the things we really value about the project. Certain specialised elements naturally travel with YE’s production so the show can maintain its technical and creative standards. At the same time, a stadium production of this scale needs significant Indonesian involvement across production, logistics, venue operations, security, hospitality, transportation, and other areas.

We are not putting a specific percentage on that split because the production continues to evolve as we move closer to the show. What matters most is how both teams work together. Indonesian professionals gain firsthand experience alongside an international touring production, while the international team benefits from local expertise and knowledge of the market. That exchange is important for us because the goal is not only to deliver one great concert, but also to build experience and capability that can support future world-class productions in Indonesia.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Raw Vision Collective (@rawvision.collective)

Raw Vision Collective describes itself as a purpose-driven cultural collective rather than simply an event promoter. What does that distinction mean in practice?

Raw Vision Collective was established with the belief that live music can offer more than a conventional concert experience. We see ourselves not simply as a promoter, but as a creative collective that brings together music, production, visual culture, atmosphere, and audience experience in a more immersive and meaningful way.

That starts with the artists and projects we choose to work with. We are drawn to artists with a strong creative identity and a distinct point of view, not only in their music, but in how they approach performance, production, and culture. That can range from global figures like YE to influential electronic artists such as Jeff Mills and Moodymann, each of whom has shaped music and culture in their own way.

In practice, it also means thinking beyond what happens on stage. We look at the entire audience journey — how people discover the experience, how they enter and engage with the space, how the production brings the artist’s vision to life, and ultimately what they take away from it. Raw Vision is independent in its vision, serious about production standards, and committed to building live music experiences that feel distinctive, thoughtful, and relevant for today’s audiences.

As you mentioned, Raw Vision had already organised projects like the official BULLY listening party and Jeff Mills’ Jakarta show. How have those experiences shaped your approach to producing large-scale international events?

For every project, we pay close attention to the full audience journey, from the music and production design to the energy of the space and the way people experience the performance. Each project has taught us something different about creating a meaningful cultural experience.

The official BULLY listening party showed us the power of bringing people together around music and creating an experience that feels authentic to the artist and relevant to the audience. Jeff Mills reinforced another important lesson: when you work with an international artist, respecting the artist’s creative vision is just as important as delivering the production to a world-class standard. Those projects also helped us strengthen our understanding of production, audience experience, and collaboration between international and Indonesian teams.

YE LIVE IN JAKARTA is obviously on a completely different scale, but the principle is still the same: understand the artist’s vision, build the right team around it, and create an experience audiences will remember.

Beyond Indonesia, which audiences are you hoping will travel to the show, and why was regional tourism such an important part of your strategy?

We have been really encouraged by the international interest so far. From the beginning, we saw YE LIVE IN JAKARTA as more than an Indonesian concert. This will be YE’s first concert in Indonesia, which makes the moment especially exciting for local fans and also creates an opportunity for audiences from overseas to experience the show here.

The early signals have been encouraging. We are seeing interest from both Indonesia and overseas markets, including Singapore, Australia, the Philippines, Vietnam, even the UAE, and other countries. We are not sharing detailed country-by-country ticketing figures at this stage, but the geographical spread already shows that the conversation is reaching beyond Indonesia.

What excites us is the bigger opportunity around that. A fan may come to Jakarta because of YE, but while they are here, they can also experience the city’s food, culture, fashion, hospitality, and creative scene. That means the impact does not stop at the stadium. It can extend into flights, hotels, F&B, transportation, retail, and other local businesses.

A successful production at this scale can also demonstrate that the country has the audience, infrastructure, scale, and local talent needed to deliver major international productions, while building greater confidence among international touring teams in the market. In the longer term, we hope this can help make Southeast Asia a more natural part of global touring routes, with Indonesia playing a meaningful role in that growth.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Raw Vision Collective (@rawvision.collective)

Finally, what kinds of artists or cultural projects would you like Raw Vision Collective to be associated with over the next few years?

We are very excited about what could come next, but rather than starting with specific names, we think more about the kind of experiences we want to create. We want to work with artists and projects that bring world-class cultural experiences to Indonesia while creating opportunities for Indonesian talent, production professionals, and the wider creative ecosystem.

YE LIVE IN JAKARTA is an important step in that direction because it brings together international touring expertise and Indonesian professionals on a major production. Every successful collaboration helps build more capability, experience, and confidence for the next project.

Over the next few years, we hope Raw Vision can be associated with projects that are ambitious, culturally meaningful, and capable of creating impact beyond the event itself. For us, success would be seeing more world-class artists and productions choosing Indonesia, with local professionals playing an increasingly important role in making those experiences happen.

Singapore singer-songwriter SIZE has lent his voice to the world of Drive Thru Magic with its original song, 'Back To You'.

Written and performed by SIZE and co-written with Drive Thru Magic creator Briggon Snow, 'Back To You' was produced by Leo Zarucky, with vocal engineering by La Min Htien. The track serves as a musical extension of the upcoming Boys Love (BL) scripted fiction podcast, which follows two strangers who find connection through a drive-thru speaker box.

For SIZE, the song was conceived as more than a soundtrack to the series — it was intended to capture its emotional core.

"When talking with Briggon about how we envisioned 'Back To You' to fit into the world of Drive Thru Magic, we wanted it to be a mission statement for the series," SIZE shared.

"You have all of these beautifully flawed and complex characters who are saddled with the weight of their trauma and grief, yet choose to search for meaning and human connection. I'm eternally grateful to Briggon for believing in my music and artistic vision, and for letting my music be part of a story that touches on a human truth that rings so deeply true."

The Singapore-based singer-songwriter is known for emotionally vulnerable songwriting, soft vocals, melancholic lyricism, and stripped-back production. On 'Back To You', that sensibility mirrors the yearning at the centre of Gabe and Louie's story — two young adults who connect night after night through a drive-thru intercom while navigating grief and learning to move forward.

Snow explained that the pair focused on a pivotal moment between the characters when shaping the song.

"Josh and I talked a lot about what the song should embody, where the heart of it could really zero in, and we kept coming back to the turning point in the series where Gabe lets off the gas and waits for Louie to reclaim his agency in the relationship," he shared.

"The song feels like driving on an open road late at night: yearning, gay, and always just short of arriving...it's up to the listener to decide when and where the car turns into."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by B r i g g o n S n o w (@briggon)

Created by Snow and produced by Atypical Artists, Drive Thru Magic stars Snow as Gabe and Daniel J. Kim as Louie, alongside Danielle Kennedy and Lauren Shippen. The intimate, serialised audio drama spans 33 episodes, each approximately five to eight minutes long, with its rollout beginning on 7 September.

The series draws inspiration from the BL storytelling that has built passionate audiences across Asia, particularly titles from Thailand and Korea. Snow cited series including Vice Versa, Never Let Me Go, Last Twilight, Semantic Error, To My Star, Light On Me, Blue, and The Eighth Sense among his influences.

At its heart, however, Drive Thru Magic is also deeply personal for its creator, exploring love, loss, change, and male vulnerability.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by B r i g g o n S n o w (@briggon)

"This is the most personal thing I've ever made," Snow shared. "It was crafted to honour the rockstar women who raised me, to process my grandmother's decline from dementia, and to show my love and earnest hope for more depictions of male vulnerability in media."

Japanese live dinosaur experience DINO-A-LIVE is bringing its premium production, DINOSAUR ODYSSEY, to Singapore for the first time. The show will take over Resorts World Convention Centre at Resorts World Sentosa from 3 to 6 December, marking its first large-scale indoor production outside Japan.

The approximately 70-minute production will feature 15 life-sized dinosaurs roaming through the performance space, allowing audiences to see the creatures from remarkably close range. The line-up includes the Stegosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Ankylosaurus, Parasaurolophus, Utahraptor, Triceratops, Suchomimus, Tyrannosaurus, Dakotaraptor, and Allosaurus.

Rather than presenting the dinosaurs as static displays, DINOSAUR ODYSSEY brings them to life alongside music, dance, immersive visuals, and theatrical effects. The creatures are powered by DINO-TECHNE, self-supporting dinosaur-type mechanical suits developed by Japanese company ON-ART over more than two decades. The technology recreates details such as blinking eyes, shifting muscles, and subtle body movements to heighten the sense of realism.

The Singapore run follows the production's premiere in Japan, where performances drew more than 25,000 attendees. Each Singapore show will accommodate approximately 3,000 guests, with the production expected to welcome more than 30,000 people across its run.

Fans looking for an even closer encounter can also add on a T-Rex Photo Experience. Limited to 100 slots per show, the S$30 experience offers a professional photo with a 12-metre-long, life-sized Tyrannosaurus Rex. Up to eight people can be included in each photo, with guests also receiving a printed photograph and an Edokko Dinosaur Mini Plate – Flower Dragon.

The prehistoric experience will extend beyond the show itself. DINO Mart will feature more than 100 dinosaur-themed items from Japan, including figures, collectibles, educational toys, stationery, lifestyle accessories, home décor, and fossil replicas. Meanwhile, DINO Café at Senmo Coffee will offer a limited-edition dinosaur-themed food and beverage menu alongside exclusive merchandise.

Singapore is gearing up for a major week in the global crypto calendar.

TOKEN2049 Singapore will return to Marina Bay Sands on 7–8 October, bringing together an expected 25,000 attendees from more than 7,000 companies across 160 countries. The event is also set to feature 500 exhibitors and 300 speakers.

The first 100 speakers announced include Shayne Coplan, Founder and CEO of Polymarket; Jeff Yan, CEO of Hyperliquid Labs; Adena Friedman, Chair and CEO of Nasdaq; Jenny Johnson, CEO of Franklin Templeton; Eric Trump, Executive Vice President of The Trump Organization; Raoul Pal, Co-Founder and CEO of Real Vision; and Tom Lee, Managing Partner and Head of Research at Fundstrat.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by TOKEN2049 (@token2049)

This year's edition will place a major focus on institutional participation, with senior leaders from BlackRock, J.P. Morgan, Morgan Stanley, Nasdaq, NYSE, CME, and Franklin Templeton expected to take part.

Beyond talks and panels, TOKEN2049 will take over all five floors of Marina Bay Sands, transforming the venue into a festival-scale space encompassing networking, wellness, live experiences, and hospitality.

The main event will form part of TOKEN2049 Week, which is expected to see more than 1,000 events take place across Singapore, ranging from conferences and hackathons to investor gatherings, meetups, and networking receptions.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by TOKEN2049 (@token2049)

Other gatherings scheduled for the same week include Digital Asset Summit Asia, Sui Basecamp, The Network State Conference, Milken Institute Asia Summit, and Forbes Global CEO Conference, alongside the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix.

“With our Dubai edition moving to 2027, our full focus this year is on Singapore,” TOKEN2049 Co-Founder Alex Fiskum said. He added that more than 70% of the exhibition floor had already been secured, with new tracks and formats set to be unveiled as the event expands the institutional side of its programme.

TOKEN2049 Singapore will also host the second edition of TOKEN2049 Origins, a 36-hour hackathon, as well as the return of the NEXUS Startup Competition. According to organisers, registrations and applications for both programmes are already running ahead of last year's numbers and have reached the thousands.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by TOKEN2049 (@token2049)

Finalists in the startup competition are set to be judged by venture capital firms Dragonfly, Multicoin, and Maelstrom.

Happy Bird tickets are currently available for a limited time, with organisers expecting TOKEN2049 Singapore to sell out ahead of the event. Limited exhibition and partnership opportunities also remain.

items.body: From Finland with love. A couple of glasses of kossu, a book of Arto Paasilinna, a record of the hardcore punk legends Kaaos, and then a movie (Calamari Union, yes) of Aki Kaurismaki, our true Homeric hero, have always been more than enough to attest to our fascination with that wonderful country. But there's more: a record label that, with the icastic name "We Jazz," helps illuminate our music like a sonic aurora borealis. The operational branches are “We Jazz Records”, established in 2016 to present "cutting-edge music on the jazz continuum in various formats, with vinyl being the primary format," and its younger sibling, “Other Power,” "a platform of all great music that doesn't logically fall under the scope of We Jazz." Both labels are curated and designed by Matti Nives. Should it be not enough satisfactory, then know that a quarterly magazine (actually a real glossy volume with color photographs) guarantees you the best editorial coverage of jazz/free/impro music available out there. For those not yet familiar with Helsinki’s alleys, we'd like to map the area with three, red marked, albums from the catalog: Mike Reed, "The Separatist Party"; Cosmic Ear, "Traces"; and Pat Thomas & XT, "Strata, Act." Completely different records with an enormous musical profile as a common factor, they represent an artistic asset value able to guarantee immortality to any label. We Jazz's new initiative includes the digital release of 5 tracks per month by bands not part of its roster, for the benefit of Bandcamp subscribers, and the kick-off is provided by this compilation which, with volumes 1-3, covers the period from January through March. We are dealing with such a cornucopia of music that it's worth a quick overview of all the musicians involved. UUSI AIKA (Sammaltuka). Strings, harp, wind instruments, drive the listener towards Finnish woodland mythology, Indian raga-inspired colors and Asian minimalism. HENRIETTE EILERTSEN TRIO (Fly Ikaros). Flautist's new band delivers a captivating composition with balanced interactions that at the same time manages to be intimate and almost limitlessly expansive. LAU NAU (Kosmospyorat). Synth drones mesh with the sound of a living garden, bees buzzing along beneath singing birds while simple chords carry dreams on oscillating waves. FELIX ALEXANDER LYBECK (Slapat Allting Hem). The magic of a Nordic forest, strange, weird folk notes intertwined with indie intimacy, creating music that feels both grounded and unearthly. JYVASKYLA WORKSHOP BAND 1970 (Nadaswaram). A previously unissued post-bop gem, this concert captures a set of groovy, adventurous and exotic compositions that firmly placed Finland on the global jazz map. LINNEA TALP (She came out of the white fog). The pipe organ is pushed in an unusual manner that allows the instrument's character to be revealed, gently, patiently, as though being teased out of hiding. ALAN BRAUFMAN (Angels). Alto sax and flute, among the actors of the 70s "loft" scene in New York, he returns after a long hiatus to lead an all star team (Patricia Brennan, Luke Stewart and Chad Taylor) between post-bop and oriental influences. FYSIIKKA & KEMIA (Luontokokemuksia). “Rural psych-jazz improvisations by Finnish bastard sons of Arbete & Fritid". Or, free music beyond the threshold where Swedish prog and Finnish weirdness collide. PIETU ARVOLA (Kummallinen ilmestys). Experimental tools like the daxophone and a dual looper called Coquantus are used to process textures combined with modular synths. MARK HARWOOD (The Course of a Year). Australian born, Berlin based, he runs a platform that works at the intersection of experimental music, performance, literature and visual art. GARD NILSSEN ACOUSTIC UNITY (Acoustic Unity). The sound of the sublime trio wrapped in the brutalist architecture and the magnetic audience of Barbican Centre, London 2018, delivers sheer, top notch, jazz aesthetic. HATKA (Peace Piece). Free, electro-acoustic textures and raw impro for an intense and playful outcome by a Transatlantic ensemble of three seasoned improvisers. KADI VIJA (Hands). A vocal instrumentalist who treats the human voice as a horn or a rhythm machine, here accompanied by piano, synth, vibraphone and percussions. PHARDAH (Village of Skulls). Featuring veterans of the Finnish experimental music and free jazz scene, along with a younger generation drummer, to unleash a vigorous bass riff, eventually accelerating into a wild collective gallop. If you're looking for a way (one of a zillion…) to epitomize in 1 hour what “Free” in music means, this compilation could be the perfect spot to pitch your tent. For our part, we already put in the collimator Vol. 2, sure thing. Check it out on Bandcamp . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Intakt Records, 2026 Personnel - Kaja Draksler: piano; Petter Elder: bass; Christian Lillinger: drums. The modern creative European trio Punkt Vrt. Plastik — comprising Slovenian pianist Kaja Draksler, Swedish bassist Petter Eldh, and German drummer Christian Lillinger — releases its fourth album. All three artists contribute compositions, adhering to unyielding rhythmic intricacy and classical melodicism to shape music that bristles with provocative interplay, freedom, and heightened expressiveness. Draksler's " Yogen " thrives on a half-step-shifting, mystery-inducing pulse. The pianist opts for motivic figures while the drummer moves from erratic fibrillation to deliberate syncopated fragmentation. This taut flow is regularly interrupted by pacifying jazztronica sections that contrast with the more Rage Against The Machine-inspired thrill of the opening. While Eldh's " Mariatorget 87 " also takes a distinctly jazz path, Lillinger's "For Sybille" finds Draksler veering toward a modern classical direction, rich with intervallic friction. The classical influence runs throughout the album but peaks with Eldh's arrangement of " När Världens Hopp Förtvinat Stod ”, a Lutheran chorale written in 1589 by German clergyman and composer Johannes Rhau. Draksler's 4/4 minor-mode piano movements find perfect backing from bass and drums. The classical vein continues on " Mere Punkt ”, co-composed by Draksler and Eldh, but shifts sharply for Lillinger's skittish “ Vrt ", which closes the album with a gallant composure. Eldh's "Trip" is one of the most gripping pieces, unfurling an oblique groove under a defiant time signature. Despite the complexity, the trio locks together in a fantastic, hooked-up rhythmic flow charged with creative harmonic progressions and tension. If " EKV " sounds progressive and warped, " For A / Kompress " is lyrical, cyclic, and powerful, opening with a dreamy aura that, handled with a firm grip, gradually intensifies. Surprising is hearing the trio lean into a hard-swinging juncture on " Granular Navigation ". Lillinger, unapologetic about his triplet-based ride cymbal patterns, wrote the piece; he also offers methodical snare buzz rolls that color a more abstract passage built from clustered chordal angularity. Punkt Vrt. Plastik engages in absorbing conversations of rhythm and breath, threading in occasional head-nodding grooves that arrive with atypical shapes and feels. The trio continues to seek new perspectives on composition, taking a freewheeling approach throughout. Kompress even offers a wider lens, feeling thoroughly contemporary without burying its influences from other eras. It stands as a fine addition to the group's catalog of state-of-the-art albums. items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur. Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.

The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album

Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
